questions.q: What is the value of compressibility factor Z for an ideal gas, and what does Z = PV/nRT represent physically?
questions.a: For an ideal gas, Z = 1 at all temperatures and pressures. Z represents the ratio of actual molar volume of a gas to the molar volume it would have if it behaved ideally at the same T and P. A wrong answer (e.g., Z = 0 or Z = RT/P) reveals the student confuses Z with the ideal gas equation itself or doesn't understand Z as a dimensionless deviation parameter.

questions.q: Explain why the compressibility factor Z for nitrogen gas at 273 K first decreases below 1 and then increases above 1 as pressure increases from 1 atm to 1000 atm.
questions.a: At low to moderate pressures, intermolecular attractive forces dominate, pulling molecules closer and reducing volume below ideal prediction (Z < 1). At very high pressures, the finite volume of molecules becomes significant - the excluded volume makes the actual volume larger than ideal prediction (Z > 1). A wrong answer that only mentions one effect reveals incomplete understanding of the two competing factors (attractive forces vs molecular volume) that cause deviation.

questions.q: Calculate the compressibility factor Z for 2 moles of CO₂ gas occupying 40 L at 300 K and 50 atm. (R = 0.0821 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹). Does CO₂ show positive or negative deviation under these conditions?
questions.a: Z = PV/nRT = (50 × 40) / (2 × 0.0821 × 300) = 2000 / 49.26 = 40.6. Since Z > 1, CO₂ shows positive deviation (repulsive forces/volume dominance). A wrong answer with Z < 1 reveals calculation error (e.g., using wrong R value, inverting formula) or conceptual confusion about what Z > 1 vs Z < 1 means. The high Z value here indicates extreme non-ideality - typical for CO₂ at high pressure.

questions.q: Compare the Z vs P curves for H₂ and N₂ at 300 K. Why does H₂ show Z > 1 at all pressures while N₂ shows a dip below 1 at moderate pressures?
questions.a: H₂ has very weak intermolecular forces (small polarizability, no dipole) and low molecular volume, so attractive forces are negligible even at moderate pressures - molecular volume effect dominates immediately giving Z > 1. N₂ has stronger London forces, so at moderate pressures attraction reduces V (Z < 1) before volume effect takes over at higher P. A wrong answer claiming both behave similarly reveals failure to connect intermolecular force strength (from c11_chem_cbse_05_001, 05_002) to deviation behaviour.

questions.q: A student claims: "At Boyle temperature, a real gas behaves ideally over a wide range of pressures because Z = 1." Evaluate this statement and explain the precise meaning of Boyle temperature.
questions.a: The statement is partially correct but imprecise. At Boyle temperature (T_B), Z = 1 at low to moderate pressures and the slope dZ/dP = 0 at P = 0, meaning the gas obeys Boyle's law (PV = constant) over a wider pressure range than at other temperatures. However, at very high pressures, Z still deviates from 1 due to molecular volume. A wrong answer treating Boyle temperature as "perfect ideal behaviour at all pressures" reveals confusion between low-pressure limiting behaviour and high-pressure behaviour.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a gas syringe and pressure sensor to demonstrate that CO₂ deviates from ideal behaviour more than N₂ at room temperature. What would you measure and how would you interpret the data?
questions.a: Measure pressure at fixed temperature while compressing a known amount of each gas in the syringe (vary volume from 60 mL to 10 mL). Calculate Z = PV/nRT at each volume. Plot Z vs P for both gases. CO₂ curve will show a deeper dip below 1 (stronger attraction) and steeper rise at high P compared to N₂. A poor answer that only measures final pressure without calculating Z or comparing curves reveals inability to design a quantitative deviation experiment.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Real gases deviate from ideal gas behaviour (PV = nRT) because gas molecules have finite volume and experience ______ attractive forces, which become significant at high pressures and low temperatures.
Fill in the blank: Observe a LPG ______ in your kitchen - it contains butane gas under high pressure.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can calculate compressibility factor Z for a real gas under given conditions, explain why Z deviates from 1 using intermolecular forces and molecular volume concepts, and predict whether a gas will show positive or negative deviation at a specific temperature and pressure.
